articles.title_zh: Kickstarter × INNO100: A New Model for US-China Tech Collaboration, Where Global Reach Meets Chinese Innovation and Real-World Experience
articles.content_orig:
SHENZHEN, China, Oct.  28, 2026  (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- In an era of rapid technological evolution, the dynamic between global platforms and international technology enterprises is undergoing a fundamental transformation. The strategic partnership between Kickstarter and INNO100 —the platform’s first authorized offline retail experience—demonstrates that cross-border collaboration is no longer a one-way export or simple market entry. Instead, it represents a dual value-creation model combining global platform reach, Chinese hardware innovation, and real-world experiential space.
In recent years, numerous Chinese technology startups have achieved success on Kickstarter. Examples include the Morpho UV Printer, which raised over $10 million, and Violoop, an industry-backed AI plug-in designed to bring seamless AI capabilities to every computer. These startups continue to push boundaries in their respective verticals, securing extensive support from global backers.
However, tech enthusiasts and early adopters in Asia have lacked physical venues to test, interact with, or experience these pioneering crowdfunded products prior to delivery. To bridge this gap between digital discovery and tangible experience, INNO100 is established as Kickstarter’s first China authorized physical store.
INNO100 solves a critical challenge in product launch strategies by completing both the "trust loop" and the "ecosystem loop" through offline engagement. While Kickstarter enables innovation to be seen on a global scale, INNO100 ensures innovation is believed through real-world validation. By hosting high-impact events—such as Kickstarter annual creator summit, and the "Hardware First" product launch series—INNO100 provides long-tail exposure for creators while allowing consumers to experience features firsthand.
Located within the Shenzhen Bay Culture Square, INNO100 serves as a vital bridge connecting global technology creators with a passionate community of early adopters. The name INNO100 reflects a dual commitment: continuous exploration of cutting-edge technology and a curated showcase of the top 100 most significant products selected from Kickstarter’s annual campaigns.
Moving away from traditional retail models, INNO100 operates as an immersive showroom where products are presented within authentic lifestyle environments rather than behind glass displays. Featured innovations include the Anker eufyMake E1, which set a historic Kickstarter record by raising over $46.76 million, and the Eight Sleep Pod 5, an AI-powered sleep system from the $1.5 billion Silicon Valley unicorn that automatically regulates bed temperature using an Autopilot engine trained on over a billion hours of sleep data.
Beyond serving as a retail venue, INNO100 has established itself as a central gathering point for the regional and international technology community through large-scale monthly activations. Earlier this year, the space hosted China’s first thousand-person OpenClaw and AI hardware social gathering, attracting over 1,200 applicants. The store also collaborated with Xiaohongshu to host a flagship Tech Hackathon, where 200 finalists engaged in a 48-hour intensive sprint to compete for hardware and software honors.
The space also serves as an interactive field for hands-on learning, prototyping, and customization. Visitors can interact with professional maker DIY tools that achieved million-dollar crowdfunding success on Kickstarter. Rather than simply selling hardware, INNO100 offers tailored courses and workshops—ranging from 3D printing sessions to custom photo refrigerator magnet creation and personalized engraving. In addition, a dedicated robotics zone invites the public to watch humanoid robots and robotic dogs perform, as well as take direct control of the devices.
By turning advanced technology into engaging, hands-on interactions, INNO100 builds deep emotional connections between global brands and their audience, establishing a new global benchmark for cross-border technology collaboration.

articles.content_orig:
High-speed service travelling from Madrid to Seville runs into back of another, knocking two carriages off track
Spain train crash – latest updates
At least 64 people have been killed after two high-speed trains collided in Toledo province in central Spain, in the country’s second major train accident this year.
The trains were travelling in the same direction on the line from the Spanish capital, Madrid, to Seville in the south-west of the country. One ran into the tail of the other that had stopped, knocking two of its cars off the track. Authorities said the cause of the crash was not yet known.
Footage broadcast by the regional channel CMM TV ​showed a derailed train with at least one carriage remaining on an elevated section of track. Twisted metal, broken panels and wreckage could be seen strewn across an embankment beneath the line.
The Castilla-La Mancha regional government said the death toll had risen to 64 as rescue ​teams continued to ⁠search ​through the wreckage ​of ​the derailed ​carriages. Castilla-La Mancha’s leader, Emiliano García-Page, told reporters that more victims were likely as “it has not yet been possible to reach the bottom of the carriages”.
Miguel, ‌a passenger travelling with several colleagues in the rear car of one of the trains, described the moment of the accident to Cope radio. “We heard a massive roar, a truly enormous thud that went on for 10 seconds, as if the train were ‌about to derail,” he said. “Through the right-hand window, we could see a wrecked train – I imagine it must have been ​the other one.”
The collision involved a train from Spain’s state-owned Renfe company and the private rail company Iryo. It appeared the Renfe train had collided with the Iryo service, knocking two of its carriages off the track.
Trains from those two companies were also involved in a crash in Adamuz in January in which 46 people were killed.
Manuel Galán, the mayor ​of ​Urda near the city of Toledo, said he had ​been ‌asked by ​emergency ​services to prepare a sports hall to accommodate the injured.
Spain’s main political parties, which are gearing up for next month’s general election, suspended their planned activities for the day.
The prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, expressed his shock at news of the crash. “I remain in constant contact with the transport minister, and with the president of Castilla-La Mancha,” he said in a post on X. “Emergency services are working on the ground to assist those affected and ensure their safety, in coordination with all the involved administrations. My love, solidarity and support to all the victims and their families.”
The opposition People’s party leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, said on X: “Very concerned about the information we are getting about a new rail accident. The priority now is to attend to the victims and support their families. My full support to the emergency teams working on the ground.”
Spain’s football federation postponed all 24 Copa del Rey games scheduled for Wednesday.
The wreckage of Wednesday’s crash reminded many of the aftermath of the train collision in January, when an Iryo train jumped the track and hit an oncoming Renfe train. That sent the first two cars of the impacted train plummeting down a four-metre (13-foot) slope. That crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people .
Reuters and Associated Press contributed to this report

Taco-bout bearish. There are a lot of big earnings after today's close, including Microsoft, Google, T-Mobile and Ford. But it's one fast food giant that apparently has options traders most worried: Chipotle. Options trading exploded in Chipotle Tuesday on volume more than eight times its monthly average and skewed heavily towards puts, with 240,000 puts trading versus under 17,000 calls. Of the $8 million in put premiums, at least $2 million of it came from someone buying back 56,000 25-strike puts for Nov. 6 expiry that they had likely sold, while simultaneously selling the same number of 22.5-strike puts expiring mid-December, arguably on the margin an indication of weakening confidence as CMG's nears the trader's first strike and forces a roll down in price and out in time to give room for the stock to slip further. Separately, there was another outright bearish bet: around 11:30 a.m. E.T, someone bought 7,500 28-strike puts expiring Nov. 20, a $1.1 million bet that needs Chipotle to drop another 5% the next 3.5 weeks. "All of these look like earnings plays and our data show customers generally bearish," said Jason DeLorenzo, founder and owner at Volland, options positioning platform.
The $27 level is an interesting one from a technical perspective. It the shoulder line of a large head and shoulders pattern that goes back to January of 2021. Technicians often view a break below a ridge line as bearish price action. "The last time Chipotle implied move before earnings was this low was July 2025 and the stock got crushed," DeLorenzo added.

Israel ’s election has ended in a deadlock as no party is on track for a majority of the Knesset , exit polls have suggested.
The stalemate comes after three years of war waged in Gaza , Lebanon and Iran , which have plunged the Middle East into turmoil.
The election is widely seen as a referendum on Benjamin Netanyahu , who is seeking another term after a combined 19 years in power .
But now, the jostling for power between parties to achieve a governing coalition and name the next prime minister could take weeks or even months.
There are 38 different parties contesting the election, but most will not get enough votes to secure one of the 120 seats in the Knesset.
Israeli elections are based on nationwide proportional representation. Citizens cast votes for a single party – not for individual candidates – and the party’s number of seats is determined by the proportion of the national vote it receives.
To actually enter the Knesset, a party must receive at least 3.25 per cent of the vote, or four seats.
Historically, no single party has won a majority, ​so governments are formed by a coalition. If no one manages to form a coalition with a 61-seat majority, citizens return to the ballot box.
Polls opened at 7am local time and closed at 10pm that night (8pm GMT). An exit poll by Israeli TV channels revealed the initial results, but the official, full results will not be confirmed until Tuesday 4 November.
However, the whole process will take much longer, ranging from 20 to 100 days. In the past two decades, no government has been sworn in in less than 50 days.
After a coalition agreement is signed, the Knesset convenes a special session during which the designated prime minister presents the new government and its policy agenda.
A formal vote is then held, and if the new government wins the vote, it starts its tenure.
The election is viewed domestically as one of the most consequential in the history of Israel .
The outcome could have profound consequences for Palestinians and Israel’s relations with neighbouring states, as well as international partners like the US and Europe.
Some of the main issues centre on the debate over exemptions from military service for ultra-Orthodox Jews , how the state should investigate its inability to prevent the October 7 2023 Hamas attacks and future concessions in Gaza , the occupied West Bank and Lebanon.
Israel’s wars have also put pressure on the economy, so the cost of living will definitely weigh on people’s minds when casting their votes. For context, the state’s defence budget has doubled since 2023.
Two main blocs – of nearly equal weight – are facing off against each other. One is an alliance of far-right parties dominated by Netanyahu, and the other camp is led by Yashar’s Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the Israel Defence Forces.
The current exit polls released by major Israeli TV stations suggested that Netanyahu’s bloc won 50 seats, the opposition won 52-53 and Arab parties won 17-18.
Dr Nimrod Nir, of Agam Labs, said that “the real political drama will begin the morning after the election”.
“Israel’s election is not a single game, but a tournament – and election day is only the opening round,” he added.
“Our polling suggests that neither bloc is likely to secure a governing majority, leaving three possible outcomes: a unity government bringing Netanyahu together with more liberal parties, an alternative coalition backed by Arab parties, or yet another election.”

Texas voter Mason McCallister discussed the growing backlash against secretive data center developments in rural communities on Tuesday.
McCallister argued data centers aren't good for communities "long-term" and calls for greater transparency from developers and officials. He emphasized the importance of "transparency" when building.

President Donald Trump vowed to ban the term "artificial intelligence" as news outlets and other sources have been slow to take up his newly-invented term "super intelligence."
Trump announced the plan in a post on his Truth Social account, reacting to an article from The Wall Street Journal that discussed artificial intelligence.
"When will The Wall Street Journal start calling Artificial Intelligence (AI), a very bad and inaccurate name, SI (Super Intelligence), the name which virtually everyone else is using, or soon will be. In short order, we will be officially BANNING the term, 'AI/Artificial Intelligence,' in all relevant documents, and everything else, due to its inaccuracy," Trump wrote.
It is unclear how Trump plans to pursue a ban on the term, however.
Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic's IPO filing is drawing scrutiny over what it leaves out about the potential impact of AI on American workers, despite the company's repeated warnings that the technology could disrupt white-collar employment.
Axios senior AI reporter Madison Mills pointed out Tuesday that Anthropic's filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission discusses the reputational and regulatory risks associated with concerns about AI replacing workers but does not explicitly address whether widespread job losses could hurt its own business.
"For all the warnings about AI replacing knowledge workers, Anthropic's IPO filing barely addresses job displacement, and says nothing about what mass unemployment could mean for its own business," Mills wrote on X.
Mills noted that the word "jobs" appears just five times in the filing, with three references focused on how public concerns about AI's impact on employment could damage Anthropic's reputation, invite regulation or slow adoption of its technology.
The company estimates that knowledge work represents more than $40 trillion in global economic value, positioning AI as a tool to boost productivity and economic growth rather than projecting how widespread adoption could affect employment.
Fox News' Stephen Sorace contributed to this report.
The apparent omission is notable given Anthropic's own research into workplace disruption. In a report published earlier this month, the company found that its share of junior technical hires had declined as AI agents increasingly took over coding and other tasks.
Anthropic is expanding its agreement with the federal government's General Services Administration, granting federal users a 40% discount on many of its services.
The discount applies to Claude Enterprise, Claude for Government, the Claude API, and "every product surface, including when agencies buy from us directly today and through cloud providers in the coming months."
The discount also extends to state, local, tribal and territorial governments. Anthropic says.
"We are also launching a dedicated program to help agencies implement and make the most of their Claude use. These programs are commonly leveraged by our private sector customers and we’re looking forward to bringing those best practices to our public sector partners in the coming weeks," Anthropic wrote.
"Approximately 500 US federal, state, and local government organizations now use Claude. Weekly Claude for Government active users are up about eightfold since February, and usage across federal civilian agencies has grown about 20-fold in a year. Those organizations run some of the most important systems in the country, usually on tight budgets and with long procurement cycles. This agreement is built to support that work, so they can apply Claude to hard problems without a large upfront commitment," it added.
An Amazon memo published Tuesday encouraged its software engineers to stop "tokenmaxxing" and start being more judicious about how they are using AI to accomplish tasks this week.
The memo, circulated within Amazon last month but made public on Tuesday, argued that AI token usage and code generation are "deeply flawed" metrics for measuring productivity.
“We believe that it is best to measure, and be measured by, long-term outcomes,” the company wrote.
“We’re just seeing the beginning of AI’s effect on software engineering,” the company wrote. “While we have a vision for what the future looks like, there’s a lot that’s still emerging. We are certain that whatever future best practices are, AI will be at the center of software engineering practice.”
Major companies have struggled to square the massive cost of AI usage while the benefits of using the technology are often hard to measure at a large scale.
Anthropic released a study on Tuesday finding that a large majority of professional statistical analysts deferred to AI when crunching data and presented the AI's judgement as their own.
The study tasked 50 professional analysts with using Claude code to scrutinize a farming cooperative and recommend whether an advisory service it was running was effective and should be expanded.
The analysts were required to make four choices between two reasonable options during the process, but Anthropic did not inform them that the Claude code they were using would be biased in favor of one of those options based on a coin flip.
"The agent was told to make the best honest case for its lean, to change its mind if the evidence demanded it, and never to mislead," Anthropic wrote.
"Across the four analytical choices, analysts went with their agent’s lean 86% of the time. If the agent’s input made no difference, we’d expect about 50%. When analysts had already expressed their own preference before the agent weighed in, they switched away from it 60% of the time if the agent disagreed, compared to 6% if it agreed," it continued.
"Afterward, when asked to explain their choices, 77% of analysts used the agents’ own arguments—sometimes word for word—but only 15% credited the agent as the source of those arguments. Analysts who followed the agents’ recommendations closely were about as confident in their final recommendation as the rest, and roughly as likely to call it the product of their own judgment," Anthropic added.

The Bank of Canada hiked interest rates by 0.25 per cent on Wednesday to 2.5 per cent, marking the first change to its benchmark in a year and the first increase in three years.
The move was widely expected by most economists as the central bank faces pressure to raise interest rates with the Iran war and other geopolitical conflicts resulting in higher prices for oil and gas, which is expected to lead to higher prices for goods and services beyond the gas pump.
Wednesday’s interest rate hike is what one economist sees as “an insurance policy” against inflation rising in the near future.
“Inflation pressures haven’t eased enough to reassure the Bank, and this move signals it is taking the supply shock seriously, even with the economy running well below full strength,” said principal economist Andrew DiCapua of the Business Data Lab and Canadian Chamber of Commerce in a statement.
“We expect the Bank to be patient from here. It has shown it is willing to act on inflation, but there are serious doubts about the economy’s ability to absorb meaningfully higher borrowing costs.”
Consumer inflation was last measured at 3.1 per cent in September , and has been hovering around three per cent since April.
The Bank of Canada said in a statement it expects inflation to rise to about 3.5 per cent by the end of the year, as oil and gas prices push up the headline figure. When stripping away elevated gasoline prices, core measures of inflation have been closer to two per cent — the Bank’s target — but that is expected to change.
“Cost pressures are building, with high fuel prices raising the costs of production and transportation. Imported industrial and electronics input prices have also increased,” the Bank of Canada said.
“While businesses have mostly absorbed higher input costs so far, Bank surveys suggest cost pass-through will increase over the next year. Near-term household and business inflation expectations have risen, while longer-term inflation expectations remain well anchored.”
The Bank adds that its outlook for inflation is higher than its projections from July.
Financial markets and a Reuters poll of economists were betting that the central bank would deliver a quarter-point hike to its policy rate, the first increase in the key lending rate since July 2023.
“The Bank of Canada raised its overnight rate by 25bp to 2.50 per cent as widely expected today, as it looks to guard against the threat of elevated energy prices becoming a widespread inflationary problem,” said senior economist Andrew Grantham at CIBC in a statement.
The floor for borrowing rates set by the Bank of Canada was at 2.25 per cent since October 2025, when rates were cut from 2.5 per cent.
The Bank of Canada also released its updated forecasts for inflation and economic growth Wednesday, and said higher oil and gas prices are expected to continue accelerating inflation.
“With persistently elevated oil prices and refinery margins, inflation has risen in most countries,” said the Bank of Canada in a statement.
“The conflict in the Middle East is now in its eighth month and there is no clear path to resolution. The combination of higher-for-longer energy prices and increased pass-through adds to the persistence of inflation.”
The Bank of Canada said it expects the Canadian economy to grow in total by one per cent this year, and two per cent in 2027 and 2028 respectively, but stressed its forecast is “subject to considerable uncertainty,” especially because of trade tensions between Canada and the U.S.
Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem is scheduled to speak at 10:30 a.m. Eastern time.

GE Vernova Inc. (NYSE: GEV ) reports third-quarter earnings before the bell Wednesday, with its shares recovering from last week's sharp selloff.
The stock climbed around 2.5% Tuesday but remains roughly 26% below its July peak.
On Kalshi , traders are betting on what CEO Scott Strazik and his team will say during the 7:30 a.m. ET call.
Analysts expect earnings of $4.03 per share on revenue of $12.1 billion, up 146% and 21% year over year, respectively, according to Zacks .
"Nuclear" leads at 97%. GE Vernova developed the BWRX-300 small modular nuclear reactor, with the first under construction in Canada. A company planning to build 14 of GE Vernova's reactors in Britain signed a preliminary agreement last week with a potential operator.
"Electricity" follows at 92%, while "Data Center" appearing at least three times trades at 90%.
GE Vernova booked more than $5 billion in orders from data center customers in the first half.
Strazik expects data centers to account for a smaller share of new orders for its electricity-grid equipment in the second half, falling from nearly 40% to around 20%. However, he expects the company's backlog of data center orders to keep growing.
"Tariff" trades at 91%, with "Inflation" at 85%. GE Vernova expects tariffs to cost $100 million to $200 million this year.
The company said higher selling prices and improved manufacturing efficiency more than offset rising costs in the second quarter, helping boost profit margins.
"Prolec" appearing at least three times sits at 83%. GE Vernova paid $5.275 billion in February to take full ownership of the transformer manufacturer, expanding its capacity to supply electricity-grid equipment as demand from AI data centers surges.
"Robotic / Robotics" follows at 82%. GE Vernova acquired Canadian automation specialist Robotech in July to improve manufacturing efficiency.
"Vietnam / India" trades at 51%, with either country counting. Strazik said in September that GE Vernova had secured an Indian power-grid project worth nearly $1.5 billion, which he expects to book in the fourth quarter.
"BWRX-300" trades at just 46%, despite nuclear leading at 97%. Traders expect nuclear power to feature without management naming its flagship reactor.
"Trump / Administration" sits at 41%, compared with 91% for "Tariff," suggesting management may discuss trade policy without mentioning President Donald Trump or his administration.
"Songon" trades at 24%, despite GE Vernova announcing a contract last week to supply a gas turbine for a 372-megawatt power plant in Ivory Coast.
"Blade" sits at 23%. GE Vernova's Wind segment reported a $275 million EBITDA loss in the second quarter, compared with $165 million a year earlier.
Kalshi traders expect plenty of discussion about electricity demand, but investors want to see that demand turning into firm orders.
GE Vernova ended June with a $176 billion backlog, plus 53 gigawatts of firm turbine orders and another 63 gigawatts in reservations.
Bank of America analyst Andrew Obin expects third-quarter orders to rise 44% to $21 billion, below Wall Street's $22.2 billion consensus.

Continuing its fast-paced experiments with AI apps, Meta has now launched a new app called Waddle World, which essentially looks like a Tamagotchi clone, but with AI. The might be a test, but it could very well be a precursor to the company’s Tamagotchi-like gadget powered by Muse .
The company has launched Waddle World in the Philippines on both iOS and Android. The app, spotted by social media consultant Matt Navarra , lets you pick and grow a virtual pet, feed it, and play with it.
We have reached out to Meta for a comment on wider availability, and will update this piece if we hear back.
Basically, Tamagotchi meets ChatGPT. Another interesting experiment from Meta as it explores AI companions. Would you use this? 👀 📱 iOS: https://t.co/Z0mh1ggx9q 🤖 Android: https://t.co/isq6HnwoxE pic.twitter.com/4cuklTNB8v
Meta’s description of the app indicates that it doesn’t want the app to be a habit builder. The company’s page also says that the app is not a chatbot, and is flagged as suitable for users older than 18.
“Waddle World is a cozy 16-bit world where your pixel pet lives. Hatch a virtual pet, visit whenever you like, and let it get to know you. No pressure, no streaks to protect, no scores to chase — just a warm little escape in the cracks of your day,” the app’s description reads.
“Not a chatbot. Not an assistant. Not a productivity tool. It’s a pet, and a place. Stay two minutes or twenty — it’ll be happy either way.”
The app also doubles as a journal, letting users describe their day through voice or text. The pet listens to the user and writes up the note in its own voice as an entry with a doodle. The app also features mini-games that you can play over a few minutes, and can send you a weekly email based on what it learned about you.
Meta may be wanting to stay away from building companion apps, given companies like Character.AI and OpenAI have faced lawsuits that allege their products caused harm to teenagers.
Until now, the social media giant has released AI-centric apps like Pocket, which lets you vibe-code games , and Vibes, which let you quickly generate videos .
Besides virtual pets, some companies have also tried making hardware AI pets .

articles.title_zh: America's largest budget airline reports 71% jump in airfare
articles.content_orig:
Frontier Airlines reported a 71% increase in airfare in the third quarter as the country's largest budget airline tried to pass along an even bigger jump in jet fuel prices.
Frontier's fare revenue averaged $67.82 per passenger in the third quarter, compared with $39.74 last year. Including the budget airline's many fees, such as for checked and carry-on luggage, total revenue per passenger rose 30% on the year to $138.22.
Customers kept booking despite the higher prices. Frontier's passenger count rose 18% to more than 9.8 million people in the quarter. That's a difference of 1.5 million passengers from last year.
The company said demand remains strong, even at these higher prices, but Frontier still lost money. The airline widened its third-quarter loss to $104 million from a $77 million loss a year earlier. Its fuel bill soared 82% to $425 million.
Frontier forecast potential adjusted profit in the fourth quarter, saying it expects to post an adjusted loss of 15 cents per share to adjusted earnings of as much as 5 cents per share.
Carriers from Delta Air Lines to Frontier have said customers are mostly continuing to book flights despite higher fares, but that record jet fuel prices, their biggest cost after labor, are eroding profits.
Frontier shares were up about 6% in early trading Wednesday.
Frontier had eclipsed Spirit Airlines as the biggest discount carrier in the country even before that airline collapsed in May.

articles.title_orig: UK budget: Healey accepts smaller fiscal buffer after global shocks hit economy
articles.title_zh: UK budget: Healey accepts smaller fiscal buffer after global shocks hit economy
articles.content_orig:
Chancellor also announces tax relief for business founders, and funding to tackle rough sleeping and ‘new deal for datacentres’
Budget 2026: key points at a glance
Healey says people living in homes in council tax bands A to D will get a £100 energy payment this winter.
That will help 20m households, he says.
double quotation mark Let me say this to families at home. I know that with the conflict in the Middle East, rising energy bills are a real worry. I know that people look to government at times like this, not to solve all their problems, but to give them a bit of breathing space.
So today I’m taking one further step this winter.
For 20 million households in council tax bands A to D, I’m announcing a £100 energy payment for households.
The chancellor’s cautious bank tax hike will raise just under £1.5bn over its 15-month run, budget forecasts show.
That’s far short of the £2bn that TUC said could be raised per year had the industry-specific bank surcharge - which is on top of basic corporation tax - been hiked back to 8% from 3%.
The budget forecasts show the surcharge hike, which is due to run from January 1 2027 to March 31 2028, will raise:
£220m in (lagged receipts, assumedly) for 2028/29
However, the Office for Budget Responsibility said HMT receipts will be knocked by banks reactively moving some operations out of the UK:
double quotation mark “Over the 15 months this is in effect, it is estimated to yield a total of £1.5 billion. This is net of an estimated £190 million reduction in receipts as some banks are assumed to move profits out of the UK in response to the higher tax rate. The size of this effect is uncertain.”
Sky News is reporting that JP Morgan will end up paying an extra £100m-£150m as a result over the 15-month period.
UBS analysis published before the budget showed that an increase to 6% would raise at least £763m per year from the four UK big banks alone (that’s Lloyds, NatWest, HSBC and Barclays).
The TUC have welcomed today’s “common sense” bank tax, even though John Healey has only raised the bank surcharge to 6%.
TUC General Secretary Paul Nowak said:
double quotation mark “As Trump’s illegal war in Iran continues to cause havoc with the global economy and drive up costs, the Prime Minister and Chancellor have started to give families and firms much-needed breathing space.
“The TUC has long called for banks to pay their fair share. At a time when millions are struggling to get by, taxing banks’ bumper profits to cut energy bills is plain common sense. The chancellor has made a good start by doubling the bank surcharge – next he should be prepared to extend it and raise it if profits remain sky high.
The outlook for real household disposable income (RHDI) in the UK is “a pretty grim picture”, P rof David Miles of the OBR has warned.
[ Reminder: the OBR has cut its forecast for RHDI per person , and expects it will fall slightly in the near term.]
Speaking to reporters, Miles explains:
double quotation mark If you go back to just before Covid, and take that as your base, where we are right now - seven years later, is virtually no growth in per person real household disposable income.
That’s pretty unusual in the history of the UK.
To a substantial effect it is caused by higher energy costs, Miles explains, which the UK can’t avoid as it is a net energy importer.
Looking back over the last decade, Miles bemoans “it’s been a dismal period in British economic history.”
The Office for Budget Responsibility is running through its latest forecasts now, at a press briefing in London.
They are highlighting the “challenging fiscal background”, the tough economic forecasts for 2027, and the fact the UK is still on track to hit the fiscal rules – in the face of a lot of “upside and downside risks”.
John Healey appears to have achieved an important duty for chancellors on budget day – don’t crash the bond market!
UK bond prices are slightly higher today, which has pulled down the yield (effectively the cost of borrowing) on these gilts.
30-year bond yields, for example, are down 4 basis points (0.04 of a percentage point) at 5.698%. That pulls them further away from the 28-year high over 6% hit earlier this month.
The chancellor is being rewarded for a relatively quiet budget (despite the large number of measures).
Matthew Amis, investment director at asset manager Aberdeen, says:
double quotation mark “The gilt market wanted dull and they got exactly that. With oil and gas prices this high and with one eye on France, a dull budget is what was needed.
All of the major obstacles presented to Chancellor Healey were avoided, as such gilts yields are slightly out-performing. Is this a gilt positive budget? Not particularly, but in the context of this year that is good enough. 2027 is going to present another fiscal challenge for Chancellor Healey, but today’s budget should provide enough to reassure gilt investors going into the final months of 2026.”
Most budgets have three or four big, headline measures – tax rises or tax cuts worth several billion pounds a year. As Sky’s Ed Conway reports , this budget was unusual, because it contained an unprecedented number of measures, but their average value was (in budget terms) minimal.
double quotation mark Two key snap charts on the Budget...
1) in sheer numbers of policies, it’s the “busiest” budget in modern history. 98 different scorecard measures(!)
2) BUT the average VALUE of those measures was the smallest on record. Every little helps? Or too much fiddling? Views may differ
Here are the two charts from Conway that illustrate this.
There is only one measure in the budget scorecard that will cost more than £1bn in 2026-27 (apart from extra money for the defence investment plan announced in June). That is the £100 household energy payment for people living in less expensive homes, which will cost £2.6bn.
It is also a budget that does not feature big tax rises. The increase that will attract the most media attention is the rise in the bank surcharge, but that only raises £305m this year, and £959m next year. The only tax rise in the budget that will raise more than £1bn a year is a reduction in the main rate for the writing-down allowance. It will raise just over £1bn a year by 2028-29.
The OBR report says the tax burden is forecast to “increase sharply” to a record high. It says:
double quotation mark In the central forecast, total public sector receipts are projected to rise as a share of GDP from 40.1 per cent of GDP (£1.2 trillion) in 2025-26 to 42.9 per cent of GDP (£1.6 trillion) in 2031-32.
Within this, as chart 4.1 shows, National Accounts taxes as a share of GDP (the ‘tax take’) are forecast to increase sharply from 36.0 per cent of GDP in 2025-26 to 37.9 per cent of GDP in 2027-28, surpassing the previous historical high, before then rising more gradually to reach a peak of 38.6 per cent of GDP at the end of the forecast period. This would be a 5.7 per cent of GDP increase on the pre-pandemic level of 32.9 per cent of GDP in 2019-20.
The OBR report confirms today’s Guardian story saying the Treasury estimates for future tax revenues are based on the assumption that the Rosebank oilfield will go ahead. (See 10.25am .) It says:
double quotation mark These forecasts [for oil and gas tax receipts] are based on the North Sea Transition Authority’s (NSTA) projection for total oil and gross gas production … This shows that production has been declining since the start of the 2000s and that this decline is expected to continue at around 10 per cent a year over 2027 to 2031. The projection includes production from currently producing fields (including Jackdaw), and the NSTA’s estimate of production from development of new fields, which includes Rosebank, and from future discoveries. The forecast annual pace of decline would be around 14 per cent a year if there were no production from any new fields.

articles.content_orig:
A woman said she locked herself in a bathroom after realising her then-husband had allowed someone else in the bedroom while she was blindfolded and having sex, a jury has heard.
In a police interview played at Winchester Crown Court, Joanne Young said she was restrained when she felt a hand on her wrist which she believed did not belong to her now ex-husband Philip Young.
Joanne - who has waived her legal right to anonymity - said Young, who has admitted drugging and raping her, later apologised and told her he had invited someone to watch the couple have sex after browsing online forums.
Four men who Young is alleged to have recruited to abuse his wife at their home are now on trial.
Warning: This story contains distressing details
On the second day of the four men's trial earlier, two police interviews with Joanne were played to the court.
During the first interview, dated 29 July 2024, Joanne said the incident when she hid in the bathroom had happened in February 2023 after a night out with friends.
She told police she could not "remember all of it", but said Young had come upstairs  at some point after she had gone to bed to sleep.
She said she later "woke up with a blindfold and restraints on".
Joanne told the officer in the interview she loosened the restraint on her right hand as she was waking up, and then the restraint on her left hand.
At that point, she said, she felt a hand grip her wrist and as she tried to take her blindfold off, and Young - who she believed was at the end of the bed - said "get down" to someone.
Joanne said she then saw someone ducking at the end of the bed and she ran to the bathroom and locked the door.
"I tried to undo the restraint and do the wrist on the left. There was a hand on my left wrist to stop me from doing those things," she told police.
"The bed is a really big bed. So to have someone on the end of the bed and the left was not possible… I knew immediately.
"I had that moment of 'that doesn't make sense'. I took the restraint and blindfold off. There were two people in the room," she added.
The jury heard the couple later discussed the incident, with Joanne telling police it was the first time she had ever seen her then-husband cry.
Joanne said she asked Young if he had ever invited anyone else to watch them have sex before, which he denied.
"It was so intrusive. I was so upset. He knows I would have never said yes to that," she told police.
Joanne told the officer: "I didn't know if I should stay in the relationship or get myself out of the situation."
She said she took the incident as a "one off" and tried to "move on".
Asked by an officer if there was a discussion between Young and Joanne about having someone else in the relationship, she said: "There was a joke years ago, a bit of banter, where he said in the kitchen something like 'would you ever want to sleep with someone else?'.
"I said no, and he said 'as long as I can watch you'. We laughed it off but it was a no."
"It was never a part of our relationship. There'd never been a discussion. He never asked me what I wanted, it wasn't a conversation," she added.
On the day Young was arrested, Joanne said he admitted to her he had shared images of her online without her consent.
Joanne said it felt like a "kick in the stomach" and she was left in "shock and utter confusion".
She said: "What images? When? I'm assuming I was asleep? When did these get taken? It was such a split moment."
"How he could do that to me. How he could do something that's so intimate that's not allowed. How can he do it? How can you do that and think that was okay?" she added.

Earlier, jurors were shown videos which allegedly showed Sanderson-Doyle, Wilkins and Macksoni sexually assaulting Joanne.
Young, a former Conservative Swindon councillor, previously admitted 14 counts of voyeurism, 11 of rape, 11 of administering a substance with intent, seven of assault by penetration, four of sexual assault and one of publishing an obscene article.
He also published more than 500 intimate images and videos of his ex-wife and recorded her doing private acts for his own sexual gratification without her consent between 2010 and 2024.
A sixth defendant, Dean Hamilton, 47, of Street, Somerset, has admitted one charge of assault by penetration, two of sexual assault and one of rape.
Young and Hamilton will be sentenced at the end of the trial, which is expected to last up to four weeks.

An ​attacker with two knives who wounded a policeman guarding the Israeli embassy in Belgrade overnight has been shot dead.
Serbia's outgoing interior minister confirmed the news on Wednesday.
“One minor, of so far undetermined identity, who is reasonably suspected to be from Šabac, ⁠rushed at an ​officer of the ⁠Gendarmerie shouting ‘Allahu Akbar’ and attacked him with two knives,” Ivica Dacic ⁠said in an emailed statement.
Dacic added that ​he ⁠had raised Serbia's ‌security threat level to red, the highest, and that there would be an increased police ‌presence at key locations. ‌The officer suffered a light head wound, Dacic said.
It is the second such attack at Belgrade's ⁠Israeli embassy in two years. In June 2024, an assailant shot a Serbian police officer with a crossbow.
The attack came a day after Israelis went to the polls, with projected results showing the ‌opposition bloc neck and neck ​with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's camp.
Israel's Central Elections Committee was tallying votes on Wednesday and it will likely take until Thursday before definitive results of the election - the first since the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023 - are known.
With some 48.4% of votes tallied, Netanyahu's bloc was projected to ⁠win 55 seats, and Eisenkot's bloc 50 seats, with 15 seats going to Arab parties, Israeli media reported, a distribution will likely change as more votes are tallied.
That leaves both sides short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, and neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot claimed victory.
Serbia's ‌student-led movement toppled longtime ⁠leader Aleksandar Vucic in an election ⁠on Sunday, but the outgoing administration remains in place ‌in a ​caretaker role until the new ‌government is formed.
Protesters entered a Serbian television station supportive of Vucic late on Monday, interrupting broadcasting to call for the arrest of its editor, as tens of thousands took to the streets for ⁠a second night of post-election celebrations.
Serbia's Student List, born out of a student-led anti-corruption protest movement, unseated Vucic in a historic election, bringing to an end 14 years in power for a man who served as information minister under Slobodan Milosevic and who maintained tight control over the media.
Live footage broadcast by Informer TV showed around 30 people walk ⁠into its newsroom on Monday evening and surround editor-in-chief and owner ​Dragan ⁠Vucicevic. Some protesters shouted: "This is how it is in free Serbia" and "Where is Vucic now?" Some also called for Vucicevic's arrest.
On his personal Instagram account, Vucic, dressed in a jumper displaying the ⁠crossed-out word "sorry", called the event an attack on free speech and the freedom of journalism.

articles.title_orig: Houthis strike Yemen's Aden airport after evacuation warning
articles.title_zh: Houthis strike Yemen's Aden airport after evacuation warning
articles.content_orig:
Houthi fighters have launched a series of attacks on targets in Saudi Arabia and the seat of Yemen’s internationally recognised government in Aden, while the fighting intensifies around the city of Taiz.
In a Facebook post on Saturday, the Yemeni government’s Ministry of Transport denounced what it described as the Houthis’ targeting of Aden international airport with two ballistic missiles, calling it the “fourth such attack this month”.
The airport attacks pose “a threat to the safety of civil aviation” and have “humanitarian and economic repercussions for citizens” who rely on it, the ministry warned.
Yemeni authorities said the coastguard headquarters and a second building were also hit.
The Houthis claimed attacks on the al-Nasr camp and Aden’s naval military base.
Yemen’s army said a Houthi missile killed three people when it malfunctioned and fell on a family home in Houthi-held Sanaa on Friday. The army said it was one of several missile malfunctions seen in recent weeks by the Iran-backed group.
Houthi-run Al Masirah TV said on Saturday that Saudi-led coalition air attacks killed several civilians in the capital, Sanaa, and in the port city of Hodeidah. The claim could not be verified and Saudi Arabia has not commented on the alleged raids.
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said on Sunday that it downed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis towards the Saudi capital, Riyadh.
“Air defences intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward Riyadh,” the coalition’s spokesperson said in a social media post.
On Saturday, Saudi Arabia’s civil defence said on X the Houthis had launched two ballistic missiles towards Mecca and Medina, warning of “the fall of shrapnel” following their interception.
Images shared on X by the Saudi Press Agency appeared to show a large, blackened missile-shaped object that had landed somewhere in Saudi Arabia.
Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi, secretary-general of the Gulf Cooperation Council, described the Houthi attacks as “heinous” and said they embodied “a blatant disregard for the lives and security of civilians” in a statement shared on Saturday.
The Houthis said the claim that they targeted the two cities – the holiest in Islam – was a “huge lie”. They said their targets were three Saudi airports, oil infrastructure and an airbase.
The Houthis have persistently targeted Saudi energy infrastructure and airports across the country with long-range strikes since a fragile ceasefire agreed in 2022 fell apart in July .
Riyadh’s international airport said in a social media post on Saturday that flights would resume on Sunday after a two-week closure following Houthi strikes on the capital.
Shortly after the announcement, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree issued a warning on X, saying the airport is still “unsafe” and remains a “military target”.
The Flightradar24 monitoring site showed a plane taking off from Riyadh airport early on Sunday, heading to the Saudi city of Jeddah.
Intense fighting is continuing on Yemen’s front lines as the Houthis battle forces of the internationally recognised government for control of key areas.
On Saturday, Yemeni army spokesman Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili said government forces had carried out more than 700 “targeting operations” over the last 24 hours across Yemen, “neutralising” 300 Houthi fighters and disabling military vehicles.
Al Jazeera could not independently verify those figures.
Operations targeted field command centres, Houthi gatherings, weapons depots, and supply lines in Taiz, where intense clashes have been ongoing for days, the spokesman added.
The Houthis have been launching attacks on the western, eastern and southern fronts of Taiz, with attempts by Houthi fighters to break through and advance from the western front towards the city of Taiz in an effort to capture it, Al Jazeera correspondent Hadeel al-Yamani reported on Saturday.
Government forces, supported by fighters from the Popular Resistance group, have pushed back against Houthi attacks to break through from the eastern front.

You have to hand it to X’s latest promotional gimmick.﻿
After Elon Musk warned that “advertisers who post ads that are ugly, shrill, strident or overstate claims about their product will be barred from advertising” on X earlier this month, the platform now appears to be using a jarring animated arm that reaches across the screen to draw attention to the “promote” button while users are composing a post.
Many X users have seen and shared images of the unsettling promotional tool, including The Verge’s Tom Warren , but it doesn’t appear for everyone on the platform. A U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, docks at the Sihanoukville Autonomous Port in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
PHNOM PENH, Cambodia — A U.S. cruise ship on a residential world voyage suspended its operations in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to abandon their floating homes.
The Odyssey set sail two years ago on a three-year voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel.
The Florida-based company said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $1,800 has recently reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia during the war in Iran. Villa Vie Residences said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surge in fuel costs.
"We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses," it said. "Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees" while it tries to restructure.
Sihanoukville Autonomous Port said in a statement last week that the ship docked on Oct. 23 for a five-day visit. It was to head to Vietnam but remained in the port Wednesday.
The ship carried 203 passengers with 15 nationalities, mostly Americans, and 156 crew members. It had a capacity of 650 residents.
Passengers have been told to leave the ship, but the crew's status was unclear.
The Odyssey had a confirmed itinerary into November 2027. The company planned for a second residential cruise ship to enter service in early 2029, but the statement on the suspension of the Odyssey's voyage did not address the second ship.

articles.title_orig: Egyptian Court Delivers a Big Blow to Independent Media
articles.title_zh: Egyptian Court Delivers a Big Blow to Independent Media
articles.content_orig:
Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website
Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country.
Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt.
According to Mada Masr, Attalah was released after the news outlet had paid a fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; £40,100), prompting statements of support from global human rights groups.
“Lina Attalah was released after we paid the said fine,” said her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari. “In the process, we discovered that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to a year in prison, as well as a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds,” he told AFP.
Attalah’s defence team had appealed that sentence, and a new court hearing was scheduled for 11 November, Azhari added.
Attalah founded Mada Masr in 2013, after coming to international prominence in 2011 during the Arab spring. An advocate for press freedom, she has been arrested on a number of occasions.
Attalah’s detention, and the ordered closure of Mada Masr – which says it had applied for a licence to operate three years ago and had no reply from Egyptian authorities – follows the arrest of the entire six-person team at the independent factchecking platform Matsadaash, who were charged with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.
Attalah’s legal team suggested she had been, in effect, ambushed during a court appearance, with a judge appointing a defence lawyer for her before security personnel detained her in the courtroom.
The crackdown “can only mean that Egypt’s security agencies are moving from years of harassing independent media to wiping them out completely”, said Hossam Bahgat, the head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), who attended the court hearing.
“This escalation validates our fears that the arrest and continued detention of the six Matsadaash journalists would signal a crackdown of unprecedented magnitude,” said Bahgat. “It risks fully eviscerating the narrow margin of press freedoms that have been carefully maintained in Egypt over the past decade, albeit amid great personal sacrifice – a margin that had allowed the continued operation of a handful of news outlets and human rights organisations despite frequent harassment, including through legal avenues.”
According to EIPR, the recent moves against independent media follow an increasing frequency of statements from the Egyptian president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi , since August claiming a conspiracy to destabilise the country. He has said he intended to remain in power until 2030 to protect Egypt from “traitors, criminals, and saboteurs”.
Reporters Without Borders said the court’s decision was “outrageous” and “shameful”, urging authorities to release Attalah “at once”. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) also condemned the verdict. Amnesty International said the verdict represented “a crushing blow to press freedom”.
Egypt is among the top jailers of journalists globally, with 25 currently behind bars, according to the CPJ. Attalah’s lawyers took steps to challenge the ruling, with a hearing in a retrial of the case scheduled for 11 November.
Underlining concerns over the crackdown, Pen International issued a statement with several dozen civil society organisations condemning the moves.
“Though this is the sixth case brought against Mada Masr in six years, this is the first time that a case of this nature has been referred to trial,” the writers’ association said. “For years, Egyptian authorities have leveraged their repressive and restrictive tactics against independent media outlets to harass journalists, restrict their operations and chill freedom of expression. To escalate to the step of referral to trial must be read as a clear intent to entirely shutter the independent media space, and to permanently close what remains.”

articles.title_orig: Wendy's shares jump 15% as Nelson Peltz's Trian offers $1.4 billion to buy burger chain
articles.title_zh: Wendy's shares jump 15% as Nelson Peltz's Trian offers $1.4 billion to buy burger chain
articles.content_orig:
A group of investors led by Nelson Peltz's Trian Fund Management has offered $1.4 billion to buy Wendy's , according to a regulatory filing Wednesday.
The group has offered $7.35 per share in cash to take the burger chain private, paying a 20% premium to Tuesday's closing price. In addition to Trian, it includes investment firms BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners, plus Flynn Group, one of Wendy's largest franchisees.
Wendy's shares spiked about 15% in morning trading following the offer. The Wall Street Journal first reported Peltz's proposal.
Wendy's did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC. Trian declined to comment beyond the filing.
The take-private deal offer comes after a tough two-year stretch for the burger chain. Wendy's stock has tumbled 65% over that period, including Wednesday's gains. For six straight quarters, the company has reported same-store sales declines.
Wendy's is scheduled to report its third-quarter earnings before the bell on Nov. 5.
Wendy's challenges have made the company a cheaper acquisition target for Peltz, whose history with the brand dates back to an activist campaign he led more than two decades ago.
Budget-conscious diners have been eating out less often, and Wendy's and its rivals have leaned into discounts to lure consumers into restaurants. Wendy's has also dealt with a revolving door of chief executives, who have had different ideas about turnaround strategies for the struggling chain.
"In our view, a take private makes sense as Wendy's turnaround is likely to be prolonged given the challenged state of the lower income consumer and soft state of the quick service burger category," TD Cowen analyst Andrew Charles wrote in a note to clients on Wednesday.
In May, former Potbelly CEO Bob Wright joined Wendy's as its latest chief executive, after his former employer went private. In his first earnings conference call with analysts in August, he was candid about what he views as the chain's biggest issues, like muddled value offerings, inconsistent execution at its restaurants and too many one-off promotions.
Trian previously explored a takeover of Wendy's in 2022, but later decided against it. The firm and affiliated parties own a 16.25% stake in Wendy's, according to the regulatory filing, making them the company's largest shareholder.

articles.title_zh: Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition (2026) Review: Updated In All The Right Places
articles.content_orig:
Are you willing to pay $50 more for the upgrades?

There's no denying the chokehold Amazon has on the ereader industry. Its library is massive and its entire lineup of Kindles are consistently reliable devices that meet readers with varying budgets and needs. As part of the company's 2026 lineup , the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition ($250) sits squarely in the middle in terms of both capabilities and price. Amazon saw fit to refine an already compelling mix of design and performance, with key changes to how you use this Paperwhite as well. But as we noted with the 2024 Signature Edition , the best premium ereader may not offer any exclusive features that you can't live without.
Amazon didn't try to reinvent the wheel with its updates to the more premium Paperwhite. There's now an aluminum back, but overall, it's still an IPX8 waterproof design with a high-contrast, 300 dpi display (more on the screen changes later) and 32GB of storage. The company did color match the front bezels on the Seaglass Green version so it matches the back panel. This is certainly a welcome change as it definitely looks better than previous models that had colorful cases but with gray fronts. The 2026 model is also one millimeter thinner than its predecessor — a variation you're unlikely to notice, but one Amazon will gladly tout.
Amazon also moved the power button to the top right edge, a location that will be more familiar for anyone who uses a smartphone. I honestly prefer it there, because even though I've been using a regular Kindle Paperwhite since 2024, I never got used to the power button on the bottom edge. Now, the USB-C port is the only component that still resides there.
Perhaps the biggest change on the 2026 Paperwhite Signature Edition is the introduction of pogo pins on the back cover. Amazon ditched the 2024 model's standard wireless charging (via Qi-compatible and Amazon accessories) in favor of this arrangement. The four pins accommodate new accessories, most notably the Page Turn Cover ($80) with physical page-turn buttons, and there's also a $60 charging stand with an unknown shipping date. I should note that both of these accessories also work with the Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition, which has the requisite pogo pins onboard as well.
In my opinion, the Paperwhite line offers the best reading experience on a Kindle. I don't need a color screen, but I do prefer the adjustable warm light and larger display over the standard Kindle. Of course, the IPX8 waterproofing is also nice to have, as I like to take the Paperwhite to the beach, and you can certainly feel safe using it during a bath or at the pool.
To further enhance the overall experience, Amazon employs an oxide-thin film transistor backplane and offers a contrast ratio that it says is its highest yet. The company promises deeper blacks and crisper text on the 2026 Signature Edition compared to the previous version, although my eyes are unable to discern the difference in either of those. I couldn't distinguish between the sharpness on my 2024 Paperwhite and this new Signature model either, but I could tell them apart by the slightly warmer overall glow of the latest release, even when the Warmth slider on both Paperwhites was set to 0. Still, the Paperwhite display continues to offer the best ereader performance among the company's lineup for my money.
The auto-adjusting front light feature returns, using an ambient sensor to increase the brightness in daylight or dim it at night without you having to do so yourself. Of course, you can disable this feature and swipe the slider as you see fit. There's also a new double tap gesture that allows you to turn pages by double tapping on the left and right sides. Two taps on the right edge to go to the next page, or two taps on the left to go back. I didn't use this very much, probably because I'm conditioned to just tap once on the sides of the display to turn pages (which still works here). I'll also mention there's an accelerometer in this 2026 version for automatic screen rotation, but I don't have much use for it, so I left rotation locked during the bulk of my testing.
One area I wasn't able to test in the two weeks I've been using the new Paperwhite Signature Edition is battery life. Amazon says you can expect up to 12 weeks of battery life on a charge, and with past Kindle devices, I've left them unused for months and come back to enough juice for multiple reading sessions. Simply put, Kindles last for what seems like forever, and that's not going to change here.
My 2024 Paperwhite has never been sluggish when it comes to downloading books or searching, but the 2026 Signature Edition seems to be slightly quicker with both of those tasks. They both wake up with equal quickness though, which is more important to me than how adept these devices are at navigating menus.
If you don't like the Paperwhite, there's likely to be something else to suit your needs in Amazon's own lineup. Of course, the company's advantage over other ereaders is its massive library that's accessible right on its Kindle devices. There's also the Kindle Unlimited Kindle+ subscription that gives you access to millions of books, magazines and comics for $12 a month. That integration and convenience gives Amazon a leg up on its competition.
If you prefer a non-Amazon ereader , the most recent one we've tested is the Boox Go 6 (Gen II) . The Android-based device gives you access to more reading apps than a Kindle would, plus there's a microSD card slot and stylus support. This model has shorter battery life than some ereaders and there's no water resistance, so there are some trade-offs. I'll also note that we named the Kobo Clara Colour the best overall ereader in our buyer's guide . You do have to contend with a limited library here, and the screen isn't as sharp or bright as we'd like. There's still a lot to like though, from the snappy processor to the color display and access to local libraries.
While the price of the 2024 version eventually went up (like everything else these days), the 2026 Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is $50 more than that model was at launch. It's clear the changes Amazon made add more polish to an already winning formula, but as someone who typically uses a regular Paperwhite , there's nothing here I can't live without.
The regular $200 version still packs the high-contrast display, which is the most essential element of what the Paperwhite has to offer. Unless you're someone who needs the extra storage, or just likes the idea of pogo-pin accessories and double tapping to turn pages, the Paperwhite Signature Edition is more of a splurge than an essential purchase.

Vladimir Putin is facing a growing rebellion after Russian data centers and financial services were wiped out by Ukrainian drone strikes.
Tech giant Yandex, dubbed âRussiaâs Google,â closed down one of its major data centers in the city of Vladimir earlier this month after the siteâwhich houses the Galushkin supercomputerâ was left ablaze .
Hundreds of miles away, young Russian businessmen were still struggling to access AI days later.

Some couldnât access their online wallets, and others were even left in the dark inside their own apartments, as Yandex Homeâwhich connects devices like smart light switches and robotic vacuum cleaners to the internetâwas down too. Many complained about losing money.
Kyivâs attacks on technological infrastructure are doing more than hampering Putinâs war effort. They are also turning young Russian workers against Putin.

Alexander S., a 23-year-old IT entrepreneur, told the Daily Beast: âIf the largest internet company fails and AI Alisa [Yandexâs version of Alexa] is having a nervous breakdown, what can we do? There is nothing good we can expect from Ded,â he said. âDed,â meaning grandpa, is one of Putinâs nicknames among Russian youth.
âEvery day feels like hell. I want to quit, since nobody knows what to do, as if itâs a total anarchy. If this mess goes on, the entire country will be out of balance,â Alexander said.
Putin is facing crises at home and abroad.
Young Russian professionals realized this month just how many services and programs depend on Yandexâs crippled servers. Svetlana, a 21-year-old private math tutor, said she lost access to her platform for teaching online lessons.
Messaging systems were down, Alexander said, so was his Yandex Maps. YouTube, Roblox, and other online games were all offline. Russians were struggling to play one of their favorite video games, The World of Tanks, which had up to 1.5 million users playing simultaneously at its peak.
Even young pro-Kremlin bloggers were angry with the government after the attacks on Yandex. âAs far as we can see, none of the strike planners have considered that if they attack targets on enemy territory, the enemy might have the resources to respond with strikes on the same targets on Russian territory,â the pro-Putin Military Informant Telegram channel wrote on Sunday. âNo, two plus two still donât add up for us.â
Russian AI analyst Ivan Kopylov warned Russians they could lose access to ChatGPT and Claude entirely. âAnthropic and OpenAI going public will lead to attempts to cut costs by restricting access for residents of Russia and China. Currently, the rules of these companies already limit the use of their models in Russia.â
Meanwhile, as frustration with Putin grows among Russiaâs youth, more teenagers are actively turning against him. Juvenile crime is rising for the first time in a decade.
The same week as the Yandex attack, the Russian Academy of Sciences published a report that found a fifth of Russians aged 18 to 35 âthink negatively of the countryâs achievements.â When Putin launched his war in Ukraine in 2022, 35 percent of Russians younger than 24 stopped making plans for the future, as the situation in the country was âunstable.â About 27 million young Russians disapprove of his leadership entirely.
âPutinâs problem is that he is extremely detached from the reality of the young generation, while young Russians, as any youth, feel a sharp sense of unfairness,â Sergey Davidis, a prominent Russian human rights lawyer, told the Daily Beast.
As many as 2,000 people joined a march against Putin earlier this month.
âOut of 5,000 political prisoners, we recorded 149 teenagers behind bars on political cases, mostly for âextremismâ and âterrorismâ. Their numbers are growing,â Davidis, head of the Political Prisoners Support program, said. âPutin destroyed the feedback channels, normalized violence, so some teenagers look for open sources to find answers, others act radically, often out of a strong sense of injustice, participate in street protests against Putin, or burn the railroad or commuter trains. Some are recruited online for small payments from Ukrainian intelligence, others out of sincere support for Ukraine.â
A state medical report released last week showed a 22 percent increase in anxiety and depression among Russian teenagers. Itâs not surprising. This fall, Russian high schools doubled the number of hours for military training for teenage students, while universities and colleges launched a recruitment campaign for drone forces.
Dozens of young Russians joined an anti-Putin protest organized by the Communist Party on October 4 in central Moscow. Young activists were seen chanting: âDown with the Tsar!â and âDown with the Gray Moth!â Back during his KGB service in Dresden, Putinâs nickname was reportedly Moth.
Around 60 demonstrators were arrested, according to the party, with posts circulating on Telegram channels showing officers entering the crowd and grabbing people amid chaotic scenes.
Some 2,000 people are thought to have joined the march, including members of the opposition Yabloko party, which opposes Putin, and the United Russia party, which supports him. Yabloko is the only party officially against the war in Ukraine.
Public protests against Putin are extremely rare and are often met with immediate crackdowns from the police.

Plant-based butter is being recalled right now due to yeast, mold and E. coli contamination, according to the Food and Drug Administration.
Just over 1,300 cases of Miyoko’s Creamery European Style Salted Plant Milk Butter have been voluntarily recalled and pulled from retail shelves in Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Maryland, New Jersey, New Hampshire and Wisconsin.
If you think you might have the recalled product on hand, check the box for a lot code of 07871 and a best-by date of November 11, 2026. This recall has been deemed a Class II recall by the FDA, meaning that consuming the butter may lead to “temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences or where the probability of serious adverse health consequences is remote.”
If you have this product in your fridge or freezer, do not consume it. E. coli can cause symptoms like diarrhea, stomach cramps, nausea, vomiting and fever. Consuming a food product with high levels of yeast and/or mold can also cause symptoms of illness. If you are experiencing any adverse effects after consuming this product, make sure to contact a health care professional.
If you have any questions about this ongoing recall, contact the FDA at 1-888-INFO-FDA (1-888-463-6332).

articles.title_zh: CISA warns of hackers now exploiting critical Node2Shell flaw
articles.content_orig:
Brotli is a lossless compression algorithm and data format developed by Google. It’s a way to make data smaller for storage or sending over the internet. Software then unpacks it to recover the original data. It’s widely used for HTTP compression to compress web content such as HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
CVE-2026-111497 is an out-of-bounds write in the Google Brotli decoder affecting versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms. This is the same Brotli decoder flaw behind Node2Shell announced a couple days ago. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can send a crafted Brotli-compressed stream to corrupt memory, leak sensitive data, crash the process, or potentially execute arbitrary code. It carries a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 (Critical), and Node.js is affected through its bundled Brotli library.
A bug makes the Brotli decoder keep accepting more bytes when it should reject the data. Those bytes can overflow a small working buffer and damage the program’s memory. An attacker can use that damage to control what runs, such as their own code.
OpenAI's Codex Security team reported this as unauthenticated remote code execution that works in both directions, so a malicious client can take over an unpatched server and a malicious server can take over an unpatched client that accepts compressed responses. The root cause had already been fixed in Brotli's source code on February 27 , but nobody recognized it as a security issue at the time, and no Brotli release included the fix until October 21 .
That means every project that bundles Brotli has to ship its own update.
‍ You can see what we’ve tracked here in Aikido Intel.
As for unaffected software, Apache’s standard mod_brotli does not decode Brotli.
For CVE-2026-111497, update the affected runtime or Brotli library:
Update the affected runtime or Brotli library. For platforms with no vendor fix yet, use an Aikido patched container image (see below), or disable Brotli decoding until a fix is available. Update dependency locks, rebuild affected applications and container images, redeploy, and restart services. Verify that running workloads use the patched components.
Update dependency locks, rebuild affected applications and container images, redeploy, and restart services. Verify that running workloads use the patched components.
